passage: I'm Gurleen, Anand's didi, and I saw the whole thing. Mummy's office friends came for lunch on Sunday. Before they arrived she told Anand, nine: sit straight, no running, no talking with food in your mouth, guests eat first. Anand nodded like a soldier. He passed the chole, said 'Thank you, Aunty,' and even laughed at their boring jokes. But when the gulab jamuns came out, the guests took four each and the bowl came back empty. Anand's face went very still. He said nothing. The minute the door closed, he flopped on the sofa, kicked off his socks and shouted, 'Finally! Now can I be normal?' I think he was only half joking.

qa.q: What happened to the gulab jamun bowl?
qa.a: The bowl came back empty.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when the gulab jamun bowl came back empty?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and resentful, though he kept his face still and said nothing in front of the guests.

qa.q: What could Mummy do next time to make guest days feel fairer to Anand?
qa.a: Set aside a few gulab jamuns for him beforehand and thank him afterwards for his effort, so good manners don't cost him his favourite sweet.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Anand's shout of 'Now can I be normal?'
qa.a: Gurleen thinks it was only half a joke, reading it as a real sign that being on show for the guests was tiring for him.

grounding: Shows a child told to sit properly, stay quiet and let guests eat first, who misses a favourite sweet and feels the gap between the home's public and private faces.

passage:
Thursday: Mumma lays out the rules for Saturday's dinner with Papa's new boss. 'Sit properly, speak only when asked, and guests eat first.' Trisha, ten, rolls her eyes but nods.
Saturday: Trisha sits straight in her ironed frock for two hours. The paneer tikka she helped marinate goes round the guests twice and is finished before it reaches her. She smiles, says, 'No, thank you, I'm full,' and her stomach growls.
Monday: At recess Trisha tells her friend Disha, 'At home we have two faces. One for guests and one for us.' Disha laughs. 'Same. Our real face eats standing up in the kitchen.'

qa.q: Which dish did Trisha help marinate?
qa.a: The paneer tikka.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she said, 'No, thank you, I'm full'?
qa.a: She felt hungry and quietly resentful, hiding her disappointment behind a polite smile while her stomach growled.

qa.q: What could Mumma do so Trisha doesn't miss the dish she helped make?
qa.a: Keep a small portion aside for Trisha before serving, and let her mention that she helped make it, so she feels included.

qa.q: What does Disha's reply suggest about how Disha sees guest days?
qa.a: Disha recognises the same two faces at home, polite for guests and relaxed in private, and treats it with humour.

grounding: Illustrates a child told to sit properly, stay quiet and let guests eat first, who misses a favourite dish and notices that home has a public face and a private one.

passage:
Arnab, sulking because the guests finished the fish fry? Sit. Let your Lavanya Paati tell you about the payasam.

When I was ten, in Thanjavur, important guests came to see my elder sister. Amma made me wear my stiff silk skirt, sit on the mat with my knees together, and not say one word. Guests ate first, of course.

I watched them finish the whole vessel of payasam. My favourite. I smiled on the outside and burned on the inside.

After they left, I cried to Appa that the house was a stage and I was a doll on it.

He didn't scold. He scraped the vessel and gave me the last spoonful. "Outside face for guests, inside face for us," he said. "Both are true. Now eat."

qa.q: What did the guests finish?
qa.a: They finished the whole vessel of payasam.

qa.q: What was young Lavanya feeling as she watched the guests eat?
qa.a: She felt resentful and hurt, smiling on the outside while burning inside at losing her favourite dish.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Lavanya accept the guest rules?
qa.a: Appa didn't scold her; he gave her the last spoonful and explained that the house has an outside face and an inside face, both true.

qa.q: How might Appa have seen Lavanya's tears?
qa.a: Appa saw a child who had held herself together all evening, and wanted to comfort her rather than punish her.

grounding: Shows a child told to sit properly and let guests eat first, resenting the lost favourite dish and learning that home has a public and a private face.

passage:
Monsoon rain kept Manjula Aunty and her three children stuck in the one-room flat in Pune for the whole evening.

"Sit properly, Sharmila," Aai whispered. "No sprawling. And guests first."

So Sharmila sat on the edge of the bed with her feet together, smiling politely, while the cousins ate the gulab jamuns she had helped fry that morning. One, two, three. Gone. She had been saving one in her mind all day.

She said "Yes, Aunty" and "No, Aunty" and nothing else for three hours.

When the rain stopped and the door closed behind them, Aai flopped onto the bed. Baba loosened his collar. Everybody laughed at once.

Then Aai opened the steel box on top of the fridge. Two gulab jamuns, hidden. "For the best-behaved girl in Pune."

qa.q: For how long did Sharmila say only 'Yes, Aunty' and 'No, Aunty'?
qa.a: For three hours.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling as the cousins ate the gulab jamuns?
qa.a: Sharmila felt resentful and disappointed, smiling politely while losing the sweets she had helped fry.

qa.q: What did Aai do that eased the evening for Sharmila?
qa.a: She noticed the sacrifice and had saved two gulab jamuns, rewarding Sharmila once the guests left.

qa.q: How might Aai feel when she flops onto the bed?
qa.a: Aai is probably tired and relieved, dropping the polite public face just as Sharmila can.

grounding: Shows a child made to sit properly and let guests eat first, missing a favourite sweet, and seeing the family's public and private faces.

passage:
Papa's new boss was coming to dinner, and the flat in Indiranagar had never been so clean.

"Ira, sit straight, say namaste, and don't talk about school fights," Mummy said. "And guests take the biryani first."

Ira sat. She watched Mr Rao take a second helping, then a third, until only rice and one lonely potato were left. That was her potato.

Her father, Nilesh, laughed at every one of Mr Rao's jokes, in a voice Ira had never heard before, deep and careful.

When the car finally pulled away, Nilesh collapsed on the sofa and loosened his tie. Ira stood in front of him and said, in the deep careful voice, "Ha ha, very good, sir."

Mummy snorted. Papa threw a cushion at her, laughing. "Okay, okay. Tomorrow I'll make you your own biryani."

qa.q: What was left after Mr Rao's third helping?
qa.a: Only rice and one lonely potato were left.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she watched Mr Rao eat?
qa.a: Ira felt resentful and annoyed at losing the biryani, and her potato, to the guest.

qa.q: How did Papa respond to Ira's teasing, and why did it help?
qa.a: He laughed and promised her own biryani tomorrow, acknowledging what she had given up.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt during dinner?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt nervous and careful, putting on a public voice to impress his new boss.

grounding: Shows a child told to behave and let a guest eat first, resenting the lost dish and noticing the family's public face versus its private one.

passage:
"Noor, beti, Joseph uncle's family is coming at seven. Sit properly. No feet on the sofa."
"Can I show them my drawings?"
"Only if they ask. And don't interrupt the grown-ups."
"Is the chicken 65 for us?"
"Guests eat first. Then us."
At dinner, Noor sat very straight. She watched Joseph uncle take a third helping of chicken 65. Then his son took the last pieces. Noor's stomach growled. She said nothing, the way Mummy wanted.
After they left, Noor flopped on the sofa, feet up. "I didn't get even one piece!"
"I saw," Mummy said, sitting beside her. "You were so good tonight."
"Why do we act different when people come?"
Mummy thought. "Home has two faces, na. One for guests, one for us." She opened the fridge. "And this face kept some chicken aside for you."
Noor squealed.

qa.q: What time was Joseph uncle's family coming?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: How did Noor feel watching Joseph uncle's son take the last pieces?
qa.a: She felt resentful and hungry, her stomach growling, but kept quiet as Mummy wanted.

qa.q: What did Mummy do after the guests left that helped?
qa.a: She praised Noor's effort, explained that home has a face for guests and one for the family, and showed she had saved chicken for her.

qa.q: How might Joseph uncle's family have seen the evening?
qa.a: They probably felt warmly welcomed and well fed, with no idea that Noor had missed her favourite dish.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to behave well and let guests eat first, who resents missing a favourite dish and learns home has a public and a private face.
